entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Paulo da Gama, a Portuguese navigator and nobleman, distinguished himself as the older brother and crucial co-commander of Vasco da Gama's pioneering 1497–1499 expedition, the first successful European sea voyage to India. Born into a prominent maritime family in Sines, Portugal, his participation was instrumental not only due to his navigational expertise but also his steady leadership aboard the *São Rafael*, providing vital support and counsel to his younger, more volatile brother. His quiet but resolute contribution helped lay the foundational stone for Portugal's vast maritime empire and irrevocably altered global trade routes, marking a definitive turning point in the Age of Discovery.

Commanding the *São Rafael*, a carrack of approximately 120 tons, Paulo da Gama played an indispensable role in maintaining the cohesion and discipline of the small fleet comprising four vessels and around 170 men. While Vasco navigated the political intricacies and often volatile interactions with local rulers like the Zamorin of Calicut, Paulo managed the daily operations and welfare of his crew, ensuring the fleet's seaworthiness during the arduous 27,000-mile round trip. His calm demeanor and experience were particularly valuable during the challenging stretches across the Indian Ocean and around the Cape of Good Hope, contributing significantly to the expedition's remarkable success in reaching Calicut in May 1498 and securing spices for the Portuguese crown.
